tables.how: Every paid line of the Controller's payment table, fiscal 2019 to fiscal 2027 to date, made by the Department of Early Childhood or the Children and Families Commission, plus Human Services Agency lines whose contract title shows early care (the words ECE, early care, child care, preschool, FCCQN, OECE, Head Start, CC Facilities or early learn; titles containing IFA are left out). That is the rule of the case's analysis. The lines are added up by payee, department, agreement, account and year: 1,164 rows for 157 payees. Two years are shown: the year the voucher number belongs to, which is how the case counts, and the fiscal year printed on the line. Counted the case's way the rows add to $117,667,522 for fiscal 2019 and $297,280,457 for fiscal 2026, the case's $117.7 million and $297,280,457; fiscal 2027, in progress, has $165,081,937, and $1,536,971 carries a voucher number from fiscal 2018 or earlier and is in no year's figure. By the printed year fiscal 2025 comes to $228,031,990 and fiscal 2024 to $243,618,627, against $189,315,852 and $279,836,772 by voucher number. 16 payees are people. 7 of them are paid under a titled agreement awarded by solicitation for training and technical help, and are named as contractors; the other 9 were paid for professional services or interpreting on lines that name no agreement, so the record does not show their role and their names are not printed (13 rows, $75,285).
tables.limits: A payment is money the City sent, not money the payee kept or spent on itself: the three largest payees pay most of it onward to care providers and families. The total is not all care: it holds buildings, wage supplements, family resource centres, research, software and office costs. It also holds $19,867,870 paid to 'Single Payment Payees', a name the table uses when it does not print the payee; $18,894,539 of that is booked to the commercial rents tax and gross receipts tax accounts, which reads as money returned to taxpayers of the tax that funds early care and not as spending on care, though the table does not say. Human Services Agency payments under an untypical title are missed before fiscal 2023. Near the turn of a year a voucher number dates a payment to within a few days. This list and the next three count the same money and must not be added together.

tables.how: Form 990 asks for the five highest-paid independent contractors and for the number paid more than $100,000. Listed are all of them on the returns of Children's Council and Wu Yee for tax years ending June 2021 to June 2025. A payee is named when its name matches a licensed centre's operator or a City-paid nonprofit, or is plainly a firm. 11 of the top-five places, $3,128,685, went to people, centres licensed to an individual, or providers that may be private homes; they are added together by year and not named. Returns that list no contractor at all: Children's Council of San Francisco 2025. The fund's contractors (lawyers, auditors, software firms) are not providers and are left out.
tables.limits: Five names a year are a sliver of the payments: the last column shows how many more contractors each agency paid over $100,000. The amount is everything the agency paid that payee in the year, from State and City money together. Families choose the provider. Wu Yee's lists also hold builders, a caterer and a cleaning firm, ordinary costs of running its own centres. A tax return is the organization's own statement, signed under penalty of perjury and not audited by the IRS. Its tax year is often not the City's fiscal year, and it counts money when earned or spent under its accounting method, not when the City paid. A disclosure on a return, including a dealing with an officer or a director, is what the law requires to be reported; the question is whether it is fair and approved.

tables.limits: These are maximums the State agreed to reimburse, not payments; what was earned and paid is not published. The Social Services tables never print a county: an agency was placed in San Francisco by its name, by a match to the Education Department's file, or (weakest, for Felton Institute and Compañeros del Barrio) by its position in the table. tables.how: For each of the 23 operators with a State general child-care or preschool contract for 2025-26 and an open San Francisco centre licence, the contract maximums were divided by the City's published full-time rates for January to June 2026 ($36,324 a year for an infant, $25,380 for a preschooler). 3 come to more than their licensed places even at the infant rate (Faces SF $15,550,015, 428 against 271 places; Wu Yee Children's Services $22,722,349, 626 against 535 places; Kai Ming Inc $15,368,158, 423 against 388 places) and 6 more at the preschool rate. The other rows set the largest count of children stated on an operator's latest tax return against its places.
tables.limits: A licensed place is not a child. A part-day programme can serve two children in one place each day, a contract can pay for care away from the operator's own centres, and a State maximum need not be fully earned. A count on a tax return is everyone served in a year across every programme. The test cannot be run properly without funded places and enrolment by site, which the City and the State hold and do not publish.

tables.how: All 578 centre licences in the file (family homes are not in it): 400 open with 20,650 places, 26 pending with 1,329, 20 inactive with 3,172, and 132 closed; none is on probation or revoked. A licence is marked City-funded when its number is on the Department of Early Childhood's list of 11 June 2025, a meal site or a Head Start site by its address; State contracts and facilities grants belong to the operator and repeat on each of its rows. Of the open licences, by kind of operator: nonprofit 170; private company 70; corporation, tax status not found 47; public body 31; church or religious body 26; not determined from the records 25; individual licensee 16; small centre, 14 places or fewer 15. The case says 160 open licences draw on two or more streams, 124 on three or more and 157 (7,895 places) on none; those counts include a fifth stream, facilities grants named on the Low Income Investment Fund's returns. Counting only the four streams the sentence names gives 139, 113 and 172 (8,651 places); both counts are columns here. Places in force on 1 July 2025 add to 24,933 and on 1 July 2020 to 23,800. 58 rows are not named: centres licensed to an individual keep the centre's name and not the licensee's, and centres of 14 places or fewer are not named in the extract at all.
tables.limits: A centre with no stream shown may still be paid: City and State vouchers follow a family to any provider and are paid through the two referral agencies, which publish no list of centres paid. Citations are as the State lists them, mostly for the last three to five years, and say nothing about funding.

rows.publisher: San Francisco Budget and Legislative Analyst

doc.t: Performance audit of San Francisco's early care and education programs

rows.said: The audit put the City's early-care budget at $66.2 million, found at least $995,000 left unspent in one year, and said the Human Services Agency "has not ensured optimal financial performance" by Children's Council, its sole-source fiscal agent for about $34 million a year.

rows.publisher: San Francisco Controller, City Services Auditor

doc.t: The Office of Early Care and Education should strengthen oversight of its contracted agencies

rows.said: All 91 sampled subsidies were properly granted, but the office did not review case files, and 69 of 579 subsidised providers (12 percent) "potentially had more children enrolled than the capacity allowed"; proof of residency was insufficient for 8 of 14 families tested at one agency.

rows.publisher: San Francisco Controller, City Services Auditor

doc.t: Field follow-up of the 2019 audit of eligibility screening at the Office of Early Care and Education

rows.said: The Controller reported that all five recommendations of the 2019 audit had been implemented and closed, including quarterly checks of provider capacity by the two agencies.

rows.publisher: Federal Audit Clearinghouse (independent auditor of the San Francisco Unified School District)

doc.t: Single audit for fiscal 2022, findings 2022-008 and 2022-010 on the federal child-care grant

rows.said: The district could not document 28 of 47 sampled charges to the federal child-care grant (questioned costs of $39,372 known and $6,711,381 likely) and had no written procedure for identifying and recovering fraudulent child-care payments; both findings were graded material weaknesses.

doc.t: Charges announced in a housing-benefit and child-care subsidy case

rows.said: Two people were charged with collecting over $30,000 a month in child-care subsidies through a nonprofit contractor for care that investigators say was not provided, for as many as 17 children; both pleaded not guilty and no outcome is on file.

doc.t: Single audits of the three agencies that pay the money onward, 2019 to 2025

rows.said: Independent auditors reported no findings in any of the 21 yearly federal audits of Children's Council, Wu Yee Children's Services and the Low Income Investment Fund.

doc.t: Citywide nonprofit monitoring programme, fiscal 2025 results

rows.said: City fiscal monitoring of Children's Council recorded 6 findings in fiscal 2025, 1 still open at the end of the review (invoices).

rows.publisher: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Office of Inspector General

doc.t: Meal reimbursement claims process for child-care centres (national audit 27601-0004-31)

rows.said: A national audit, not about San Francisco, found meal-count discrepancies at four of five sponsoring organizations it tested in one State and $6,672,035 of unsupported claims, and said capping claims at licensed capacity reduces inflated claims.

rows.publisher: U.S. Office of Management and Budget, PaymentAccuracy.gov

doc.t: Child Care and Development Fund: improper payment rate

rows.said: Nationally the federal child-care grant was reported 95.1 percent accurate for fiscal 2025; no rate is published for California or for San Francisco.

tables.how: City payments are the yearly sums of the first list by voucher number; State money is the counted amounts of the State contract list, on file from 2023-24. $117,667,522 over 36,864 children under five gives $3,192 for fiscal 2019, and $297,280,457 over 32,320 gives $9,198 for fiscal 2026. Adding $219,629,394 of State maximums makes $15,993 for each child under five and $20,732 for each of 24,933 licensed centre places. In fiscal 2025 the City counted 9,150 children receiving funded care: $20,690 each by voucher number, $24,922 by the year printed on the payments. The State's own count of centre places on 29 June 2023 was 24,702; the licence list adds to 25,124 for 1 July 2023.
tables.limits: Dollars for each child under five divide by every young child in the city, so they measure the size of the effort and not what a child's care costs. The rise follows the commercial rents tax for early care that voters passed, a decision of policy. State figures are maximums, not payments. The two population sources disagree, and the State's figures after 2024 are projections. Children served by site are not published.

Large-home counts are from the State licensing file of 8 November 2026, which lists only homes licensed for 12 or 14 children. tables.limits: A family child-care home is a private residence: no home, licensee or address is listed here or kept in the project's files. Money paid to homes cannot be separated from money paid to centres at any level: it is inside the referral agencies' unnamed onward payments. The City list includes small homes and the State file does not, so the two columns do not count the same thing.
